divisions.question: David Leyonhjelm by leave—I move amendments (1) to (3) on sheet 7734: (1) Schedule 1, page 4 (after line 31), after item 4, insert: 4A Subsection 90(3B) Repeal the subsection. 4B Subsection 90(3C ) Omit ", (3AF) and (3B)", substitute "and (3AF)". (2) Schedule 1, page 5 (after line 2), after item 5, insert: 5A Subsection 90A(1) Repeal the subsection, substitute: (1) This section applies in relation to a decision of the Secretary under section 90 rejecting an application by a pharmacist for approval to supply pharmaceutical benefits at particular premises, if the application was made on or after 1 July 2006. (3) Schedule 1, page 13 (after line 4), after item 31, insert: 31A Subsection 99K(2) Repeal the subsection. 31B Section 99L Repeal the section. These amendments, of necessity, work as a whole and are intended to achieve the following. They remove the location rules under which the Australian Community Pharmacy Authority makes its recommendations regarding applications for new pharmacies. They remove the requirement for the secretary to comply with recommendations of the Australian Community Pharmacy Authority regarding applications for new pharmacies. They allow the minister to override a rejection by the secretary of an application for a new pharmacy. The intention here is to remove the possibility that the Australian Community Pharmacy Authority, making recommendations on a whim rather than on the basis of location rules, would continue to prevent new pharmacy approvals. The net effect of my amendments to this bill would be twofold: first, it would allow people to open a pharmacy wherever they like, including in a supermarket; second, it would turn a mixed bill into a good bill. As I mentioned in my speech on the second reading, there are many good things in this bill: price disclosure, reducing the cost of single brand drugs and the closing of the price disclosure loophole with respect to combination medicines—a notorious rort ably identified by Philip Clarke,

speeches.speaker: Sussan Ley
speeches.brief: The government moved the National Health Amendment (Pharmaceutical Benefits) Bill 2015, implementing the PBS Access and Sustainability Package to achieve $3.7 billion in net savings over five years through pricing reforms, including a 5% reduction on F1 medicines and removal of originator brands from price disclosure for F2 medicines after three years. The bill also introduces up to $1 co-payment discounts, increases PBAC membership to 21, extends the Sixth Community Pharmacy Agreement with $18.9 billion in funding, and removes low-cost over-the-counter medicines from the PBS.

speeches.speaker: Stephen Jones
speeches.brief: Labor argued the bill was rushed due to the government's incompetence, with negotiations starting only four months before the expiry of the previous agreement and Labor not consulted until the night before the bill was tabled. The party expressed concerns about unintended consequences from the lack of consultation, particularly regarding the $3.7 billion in net savings from the PBS Access and Sustainability Package, the impact of allowing pharmacists to discount the co-payment on patients reaching the safety net, and the unclear provisions for biosimilar substitution.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Southcott
speeches.brief: The bill implements measures from the Sixth Community Pharmacy Agreement, including a $2.8 billion investment in pharmacy and primary care and $6.6 billion in efficiencies over five years, with new drug listings averaging 30 per month compared to eight under the previous government.

speeches.speaker: Nick Champion
speeches.brief: Labor supported the National Health Amendment (Pharmaceutical Benefits) Bill 2015, which introduces PBS pricing changes, allows $1 pharmacy co-payment discounts, removes some over-the-counter medicines, and increases PBAC membership from 18 to 21. The speech criticised the government for making $6.6 billion in health savings without reinvesting them, lacking consultation, and rushing the bill, citing concerns from Professor Brian Owler and Medicines Australia, and an ABC Fact Check finding that 85 per cent of $73 million in paracetamol costs is for chronic pain prescriptions.

speeches.speaker: Alannah MacTiernan
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the National Health Amendment (Pharmaceutical Benefits) Bill 2015, highlighting the need to balance PBS sustainability with access to expensive new drugs like crizotinib (for ALK4 cancer mutation). They emphasised concerns about pharmaceutical lobbying, cited the cases of Julie Sackett and Theresa Tan, and noted potential risks from the Trans-Pacific Partnership to PBS provisions.

speeches.speaker: George Christensen
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the bill implementing the Sixth Community Pharmacy Agreement, citing doubled program funding to $1.2 billion and optional discounted co-payments for consumers, while expressing concerns about the impact on small rural pharmacies and calling for monitoring.

speeches.speaker: David Gillespie
speeches.brief: The speech supported the National Health Amendment (Pharmaceutical Benefits) Bill 2015 as a balanced deal for taxpayers, industry and pharmacists, citing a one-off 5% reduction in premium prices for single-brand drugs after five years on the PBS, removal of originator drugs from combination formularies, $3 billion for the Sixth Community Pharmacy Agreement (including infrastructure and handling fees, dispensing fee growth, and funding for simple primary care in pharmacies), and expanded PBAC membership to handle increased workload.

speeches.speaker: Nola Marino
speeches.brief: The National Health Amendment (Pharmaceutical Benefits) Bill 2015 is supported for establishing the PBS Access and Sustainability Package, including $6.6 billion in efficiencies over five years, doubling drug listings with $3 billion invested in 18 months, and measures to reduce consumer medicine prices by up to 50 percent for generics and $1 per script for co-payments.

speeches.speaker: Don Randall
speeches.brief: The bill was argued to implement the $18.9 billion Sixth Community Pharmacy Agreement and the PBS Access and Sustainability Package, reducing the concessional co-payment from $6.10 to $5.10, while contrasting the government’s consultation with Labor’s earlier $800 million cut to pharmacy funding.

speeches.speaker: Jane Prentice
speeches.brief: The bill implements the PBS Access and Sustainability Package and the Sixth Community Pharmacy Agreement, including a one-off 5% price cut for single-brand drugs, removal of originator prices for multi-brand drugs, and $18.9 billion for community pharmacy over five years. It also supports new PBS listings for treatments such as melanoma, breast cancer, eye conditions, and the shingles vaccine Zostavax, with savings reinvested in the health portfolio.

speeches.speaker: Sussan Ley
speeches.brief: The speaker defended the bill as implementing the Access and Sustainability Package and Sixth Community Pharmacy Agreement, which will deliver $18.9 billion to community pharmacy over five years, achieve net PBS savings of $3.7 billion, invest $1.3 billion in new medicines, allow pharmacists to reduce co-payments by $1, and delist certain over-the-counter medicines.
